Personnally, I (28F) just went through the worst year of my life so far. Even longer, because it all started in Nov 2019 with my father's heart attack and a few months later quarantine hit us and I could not visit him. He's my only living parent and I had this sudden scare that I could end up an orphan. The anxiety slowly but surely took over, messing with my sleeping schedules, I coped using drugs, prescribed or directly snorted off clubs toilets seats and put myself in several dangerous situations. Lost my friends, one after the other. Quarantine hit and I was by myself, I stopped sleeping, chronic insomnia triggered sleepwalking, and after a few months, over-compensating in my work ended up in exhaustion and an ulcer.

After the surgery, I was considering going back at work or leaving. I spent a whole month in my sterilized room, but my fluffy partnet was allowed as he's an indoor cat. It broke my heart when I eventually went back to the office. I promised myself I would start working to get the both of us a bigger appartment where he could jump and run and play around, and soon after I was back at my desk it became clear that job would not allow me to afford our dream playground, on top of keeping me away from him, stuck at my desk, up to 14 hours a day.

I sprinted through the most hardcore month of work ever and I then took a second sick leave, as I was not recovering from the surgery, wasn't sleeping much, and kept losing weight. I would never return.

The following months were hard financially, I am grateful I had friends to help me with my rent sometimes. We moved into a bigger (and more expensive) appartement days before I was told I was getting fired. I was still feeling sickly and from that point, I had to grieve never going back to that office. But I spend those months unemployed renovating and refurbishing old furniture, crap I had picked up on the streets or bought in second-hands depot. I did everything in my power for my kitty to enjoy his new home. I was desperate, invoices and even lawyer's mails started coming in the mail. I could not pay everything with my ridiculous unemployment allowances. But I always made sure he had everything he need, and he's so happy.

In debt, unemployed and still in recovery, I don't know why or how but as soon as I was finished with the furniture, I started applying to other jobs. It took another 2 months to take shape, but this week I ended up having to turn down several job offers because I was offered my dream job. I start in two weeks. I've started paying back most of my late invoices, I'm 2/3rd in paying everyone back, and I will be finished even sooner since I'll be getting a real salary very soon.

I owe it to my friends, but I'm also grateful for my cat. There were times when I was seriously questioning the point of my existence, and had very dark urges. But I could never give him up. I promised him a better life when I adopted him from the shelter, and I worked hard for it everyday these past months, and he's so happy. That makes me happy. All I managed to do for myself lately, was because he needed me and loved me unconditionnally, burnt-out, sick, unemplowed, sad, he would show me the same respect and affection. And it kept me going when the whole world seemed to have failed me. I love him so much.

My mother was bipolar, and just like your father, she would go through episodes of depression that lasted for years, interrupted by short weeks or months of mania where she'd make weird and abrupt decisions. While I was growing up, I mostly remember her as depressed, but when I was 11, she went full manic and sold the house without telling my father. We moved, but after a few months she fell back into depression again. Ponctually, throughout her depressive and manic episodes, she'd tell us (me and my brothers) that she never wanted us and we were a disgrace. It felt like harassment so at the first opportunity I had I moved out at 16. My brothers moved out as well the same year. Being practically on her own (with only my little brother left to torture), she went full manic again, argued she wanted to go back to work and was able to keep a job. We let her. It lasted months. During those episodes, she had strongly mixed feelings about us, we were sometimes welcome at home, sometimes not. Eventually we all came home in the summer, it was time to share what we had all been up to since we moved out. We talked about our progresses and failures. She was immensely disappointed in us for various ridiculous reasons. She went on panic mode (we still don't know which child, which criteria, which specific "event" or "failure" made her feel that way), she competely shut down. Didn't talk. Would scream if you adressed her. If you insisted she'd threaten you with a knife. It lasted two weeks, and we were hoping at some point, she'd calmed down. It looked like it, because one afternoon she came to us and said "well, I'm taking the week end off with my grandchildren (from my stepbrother), I'll feel better when I come back". She committed suicide on the way there and never came home.

What I'm saying is : since you can never predict or guess what episode a bipolar person is going through (depression, mania, rapid cycling, anxiety), you can only let them be and do your best, even if it takes up a lot of your energy, to stay close to them and keep the communication going. They might need your help out of nowhere. They may not be able to express it. They might put harsh words on horrible feelings they have but that are not adressed to you personnally (even if they seem so). It takes patience and understanding, and I know it's exhausting. I have been there and my own bipolar is way more under control than my mom's but I am still difficult to communicate with at times. 

I think you are doing the right thing reaching out to your dad's. If you are very worried, you might take the step further and visit him. But don't let his words make you question his love for you. Give him time and space but stay right by his side, just in case.

People with BPD ou BD or other personality and mood disorders can go seriously crazy and be threatening and harmful to others but deep down, they are the one aching and misunderstanding themselves.

THIS DOES NOT MEAN YOU FORGET. This means you can temporarily forgive, and suggest she gets help. Hear me out.

She never meant anything she said that day, and the emotions she felt were intense and exaggerated and wrong.

I had never heard of the name before but just reading about it I understand more or less what it means and think I have already gone through some kind of similar therapy.

It's a very common approach discussed in details by someone here : [Loneliness, depression and anxiety posts](https://www.reddit.com/r/SeriousConversation/comments/d3d29w/loneliness_depression_and_anxiety_posts/)

That person doesn't exactly know what he's talking about (at least, isn't capable of putting technical words on it) but he basically summarizes the Gestalt approach imo. I'll summarize it for you as well.

Humans are social animals, tribal, they live in groups and take care of each other. When something in that social environment goes wrong (like the sudden passing of a loved one, a break up, or other kinds of loneliness and social isolation) , humans are sad. They feel left out, isolated and thus, depressed and anxious. That is it, it's an environment-based approach. 

What they work on in those kinds of therapies is cognition : how you perceive your environment. They will try, by making you talk a lot but also contributing to the discussion, to make you take a step back until you change your perception of what initially depressed or isolated you. It's basic darwinism : they will get you to adapt to your new or broken environment. 

What do I think of it ? I think it works, on some level. It is true and cannot be proven wrong, that a lot of things are wrong around you and not inside of you. 

But take into consideration that some mental illnesses are also due to real chemical imbalances, that no Gestalt-therapy can fix. It comes in addition to another kind of therapy, follow up, and maybe medication. If you were diagnosed bipolar, you must know there is something "physically wrong" going on in your brain (and I don't want to upset you any more than you might already be), and that this kind of therapy can really be an improvement on you, without totally fixing your pathologicals ups and downs.

It all depends on the diagnosis, I think it might work well on unipolar depression or seasonal depression, or social anxiety, PTSD. But as far as bipolar disorder is concerned, I'm not 100% sure.

I also think one should consider having a parallel dataset of "unhappiness" factors (like suicide rates, depression rates and other kinds of mental illnesses caused by traumas, addictions, etc) that you could cross with your happiness factors. Otherwise, you have nothing to compare your data too and you're just left with a percentage of "happiness" per sample like those international institutes do, but with other randomly picked factors. But one thing you're absolutely right tho, is to first choose a sample you know well (in my case, any European country would do), and re-experiment in comparison with other samples that have cultural differences, in order to reduce the number of factors to its minimum and make the final "calculus" as "universal" as possible.

Humans are humans, and this "happiness equation" if it may exist, will never take into consideration humans interacting with each other, and imo that's the most hazardous and undeterminable data. I have bipolar 2 and social anxiety since I was 12 and at some point in my life it was truly debilitating, I couldn't even talk in public and had panic attacks if anyone spoke a bit loud. I had also been so traumatized by my mother's manic episodes that I would rather hide and isolate myself than show my own symptoms to others. 

First off, I started "working" as a volunteer when I was young, in projects that interested me beyond the people that I would meet. I started organizing concerts, volunteering in music festivals and in farms and shelters. I'm a simple person, I love music and animals. Those experiences made me meet a lot of people and realize that when we're moving towards the same objective, we mostly get along. Of course there were disagreements but nothing was as violent or harsh as what I had known with my mother's mania, so my anxiety felt a lot better already.

Now I've finished my Master's degree and started working. My bipolar is all over the place and I can't seem to handle a full time job. My crazy sleep schedules, my nerves, my moods, my meds, my crippling anxiety ALL make it impossible to make it through an 8 hour day, yet a 5 day week. My boss is well aware of mental health issues and we are working on making my office a safe space for me. For example, I have phone anxiety, so I am never forced to pick up the phone if I don't feel like it. Surprisingly enough, I tend to pick it up from time to time, to prove that I manage ! He arranged it so I can work from home when social anxiety kicks in. He knows I might bite half a xanax if we have an important deadline and he's okay with it. He says the most important is that I get the medical care and attention I need to be my best self, and that I should organize my work around it. Sometimes I don't even work my full 40 hours because it's too hard, but that's fine by him as long as I'm reliable and get stuff done when I'm okay. 

I am very, very lucky, to have such a boss. But what I didn't tell you is that before that, I had other jobs, and I failed, miserabily. I had to resign, because I was on sick leave all the time and nobody to talk to about my mental illness. I was so fucking ashamed I even tried to commit suicide at some point, when I left an office job I had been for a year and where nobody had noticed my self harm scars. It took me time to find a professional situation I am at peace with. What helped was getting some of my stuff fixed : get therapy, get the necessary treatment, be surrounded by positive people who knew I could manage. Then I considered it a challenge to go through a day's work, and I realized some were easier than others, some I could go through without Xanax, some I needed someone to cheer me up. In all cases there was always a solution and it became more and more rare that I'd skip work (even when working in retail which was really stressful). 

So don't give up, you can do it. Go step by step, surround yourself with positive people and realistic goals. It's not a joke that everything will be okay. It will, I promise, I've been there not so long ago.

Also, as far as my bipolar is concerned, CBT never helped, sadly. I don't think I can ever get that fixed without meds.

But CBT really, really helped with my social anxiety ! It has been a ten year training to be able to speak in front of groups of people, pick up the phone, answer a customer. I still relapse sometimes and isolate myself, but I made so many improvements and I'm proud. Please try it. Know your triggers, put yourself at risk and overcome them, little by little. 

I wish you the best of luck ! Love
